Chapter 3: Facing Fear, Doubt, and the Risk of Failure
So, let’s talk about something every artist wrestles with sooner or later—fear. Not just the fear of creating something that doesn’t work, but that nagging feeling your efforts might not matter at all.
You know, that kind of fear can freeze you in your tracks, sometimes before you even pick up a brush or a pen. But oddly enough, that fear? It’s proof that the work means something to you.
Picture this—a painter sits alone in their apartment, staring at a blank canvas, hesitating to make the first mark. The memory of recent disappointments is still fresh, and the fear of making those same mistakes again can feel overwhelming.
But here’s the thing: the only way forward is to try again. That’s how you learn, right?
Fear wears a lot of different masks. Sometimes, it’s that worry that people won’t like what you’ve made. Other times, it’s the fear of not living up to your own expectations. And for some, the scariest thought of all is that their work might go completely unnoticed.
The truth is, these worries aren’t just for beginners—they stick around, even when you’ve been at it for years.
Now imagine a sculptor, working late, questioning every decision. Is this the right material? Is the shape interesting enough? Those doubts start to pile up, and suddenly it’s hard to see the piece for what it could become.
In moments like that, it’s easy to forget—uncertainty is just part of the process.
Most of us don’t realize that failure isn’t just possible—it’s inevitable. Every artist makes mistakes. Some pieces just don’t work out, no matter how hard you try. But every time something flops, it’s a chance to learn.
And after a while, the fear of failure shifts. It’s not just about the work anymore, but what those failures might say about who you are.
Think about a photographer scrolling through a batch of blurry, off-target shots. Disappointment hits hard—the pictures don’t match what they saw in their mind.
But instead of giving up, they dig in. They look for patterns, ask what went wrong, and try to figure out how to get better next time. The next round of photos? They’re a little sharper. That’s progress—learning from the mess-ups, not avoiding them.
One of the toughest lessons for any artist is learning to separate self-worth from the outcome of your work. It’s so easy to tie your identity to success or failure—to think a bad painting means you’re a bad artist.
But the real truth? Everyone makes things that don’t quite work. The important thing is to show up and keep going anyway.
In a small writing group, folks share rough drafts—stuff that’s messy and unfinished. Some are embarrassed, worried about how others will react. But as people talk, it becomes obvious—everyone’s facing the same fears. Sharing those struggles, letting yourself be vulnerable, can loosen the grip of self-doubt.
Over time, it gets clearer—fear isn’t something you conquer just once and move on from. It comes and goes. Some days it’s louder, some days it fades into the background.
What matters is that you keep working, even when fear tries to shout you down. Every piece you make, every attempt you take, is a step forward.
The risk of failure never really disappears, but it does get less scary with practice. When you accept that mistakes are part of the gig, you can focus on what really matters: making things, discovering new ideas, and feeling that spark when something finally takes shape.
